title: Schools, Cell Phones, and AI: Q&A with Melissa Kay Diliberti
gist: RAND survey data show student AI use rising across school levels, with two-thirds of students worried it harms critical thinking and only about a third reporting schoolwide AI rules. On phones, around 20% of teens check them five-plus times per class day despite near-universal restrictions, whose effectiveness is still thinly evidenced.

insights.claim: RAND surveys show the share of students using AI for schoolwork is rising at the middle school, high school and postsecondary levels.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: Sustained growth in student AI usage supports the education use case for AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT.
insights.locator: The share of students who are using AI

insights.claim: A majority of students surveyed by RAND do not consider it cheating to use AI to look up facts or get better explanations of assignments.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: Normalization of AI as a study aid suggests durable, not fad, adoption among students.

insights.claim: Two-thirds of students report at least some concern that using AI is harming their critical thinking, even as they keep using it.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: User ambivalence could fuel regulatory or school-level restrictions and demand for 'learning-safe' AI products.
insights.quote: two-thirds of students tell us they have at least some concern that using AI is harming their critical thinking
insights.locator: The share of students who are using AI

insights.claim: In a December survey, only about a third of students said their school had schoolwide AI rules, and many said they did not know.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: Policy vacuum around school AI use leaves room for vendors and districts to set norms; guidance development is a coming need.
insights.quote: Only about a third said there were schoolwide rules.
insights.locator: Schools are starting to get some policies

insights.claim: AI technology is moving so fast that school guidance is lagging and not widely known, and Diliberti argues schools have an opportunity and obligation to develop clear guidance on when students may use AI.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of school AI policy-making, creating demand for compliance, detection and education-specific AI tools.
insights.quote: Schools have an opportunity—and an obligation—to develop guidance.

themes.theme: Cell phone use and bans in schools

insights.claim: Around 20 percent of teens say they check their phones five or more times a day in class and another 40 percent say one to four times, even in schools that have banned phones.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: Bans alone are only partially effective at curbing in-class phone use.
insights.quote: around 20 percent said they check their phones five or more times a day in class
insights.locator: The other big one, of course

insights.claim: Nearly all schools now have policies restricting cell phone use, but there is very little evidence on how effective they are; more restrictive policies and strict teacher enforcement correspond to fewer students checking phones, based on self-reports.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: Enforcement intensity, not just policy existence, appears to drive outcomes.
insights.quote: But there's very little evidence about how effective these policies have been.
insights.locator: That's one of the biggest questions

insights.claim: Emerging evidence links cell phone bans to reduced phone use in schools and possibly better student well-being in the longer term, while links to achievement remain unclear.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: Evidence base remains thin; policy momentum is ahead of proof.

insights.claim: Phone bans carry real trade-offs: teachers do not want to be 'phone police' and parents are skeptical of full bans because they want emergency contact with their kids.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: Parental resistance may push schools toward partial restrictions rather than full bans.
insights.quote: Teachers don't want to spend all day being the phone police.
insights.locator: But there are also some real trade-offs.

insights.claim: Schools are in a period of real transition beyond technology, with high rates of student absenteeism and teacher stress.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: Absenteeism and teacher burnout are persistent structural pressures on public education.
insights.quote: We see high rates of student absenteeism, high rates of teacher stress.
insights.locator: This is a period of real transition

insights.claim: Media coverage of AI cheating and phone addiction is largely anecdotal, and RAND's survey panels aim to quantify how widespread these issues are and how they change.
insights.speaker: Melissa Kay Diliberti
insights.so_what: RAND panel data is a quantitative indicator source for tracking education-technology adoption trends.
